'''Sonja-Verena Albers''' is a German microbiologist who is a professor at the [[University of Freiburg]]. Her research focuses on the cell biology of the archaea ''[[Sulfolobus acidocaldarius]]'' and ''[[Haloferax volcanii]].'' She was elected Fellow of the [[American Society for Microbiology]] in 2023.

== Early life and education ==
Albers attended high school in [[Hamburg]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Zeitung |first=Badische |date=2020-02-17 |title="Enormes Interesse und Geduld" |url=https://www.badische-zeitung.de/enormes-interesse-und-geduld--182862593.html |access-date=2023-02-17 |website=Badische Zeitung |language=de}}</ref> She studied biology at the [[University of Würzburg]], during which time she completed an internship at the [[Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry]] and became interested in [[Archaea]].<ref name=":0" /> In Munich, she met a researcher from the Netherlands who studied Archaea, and their research interested her so much she moved to the [[University of Groningen]]. She completed her doctoral research in molecular microbiology at the University of Groningen, where she studied sugar transport in ''[[Sulfolobus solfataricus]]''.<ref name=":0" /> After graduating she was made a [[Dutch Research Council]] postdoctoral researcher.{{citation needed|date=February 2023}}

== Research and career ==
In 2006, Albers was awarded a Dutch Research Council VIDI grant to establish her own group at the University of Groningen.{{citation needed|date=February 2023}} She moved to the [[Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology]] in 2008, where her research interests moved to understanding the archaea cell envelope.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-11-01 |title=Snapshot: Dr. Sonja-Verena Albers |url=https://microbiologycommunity.nature.com/posts/22138-snapshot-dr-sonja-verena-albers |access-date=2023-02-17 |website=Nature Portfolio Microbiology Community |language=en}}</ref> In 2014 she was made a professor of microbiology at the [[University of Freiburg]].{{citation needed|date=February 2023}}

Albers has investigated the structure-property relationships of archaea<ref>{{Cite book |last1=van Wolferen |first1=Marleen |last2=Albers |first2=Sonja-Verena |title=Archaea |date=2022 |chapter=Progress and Challenges in Archaeal Cell Biology |chapter-url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36125763/ |series=Methods in Molecular Biology |volume=2522 |pages=365–371 |doi=10.1007/978-1-0716-2445-6_24 |issn=1940-6029 |pmid=36125763|isbn=978-1-0716-2444-9 }}</ref> and the molecular mechanisms that underpin the transmission of environmental cues to its motility structure.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Albers |first1=Sonja-Verena |last2=Koning |first2=Sonja M. |last3=Konings |first3=Wil N. |last4=Driessen |first4=Arnold J. M. |date=2004-02-01 |title=Insights into ABC Transport in Archaea |url=https://doi.org/10.1023/B:JOBB.0000019593.84933.e6 |journal=Journal of Bioenergetics and Biomembranes |language=en |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=5–15 |doi=10.1023/B:JOBB.0000019593.84933.e6 |pmid=15168605 |s2cid=22153516 |issn=1573-6881|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Archaea, one of the three domains of life, are single-cell life forms without a nucleus.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Freiburg |first=Albert Ludwigs University of |title=How single-cell archaea determine what direction to swim |url=https://phys.org/news/2018-01-single-cell-archaea.html |access-date=2023-02-17 |website=phys.org |language=en}}</ref> They adapt to extreme living conditions (e.g. hot sulphur springs, salty lakes), are found in a variety of environments around the world.<ref name=":1" /> Albers' research uncovered the structure of proteins used by archaea to decide which direction to swim.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Quax |first1=Tessa E. F. |last2=Altegoer |first2=Florian |last3=Rossi |first3=Fernando |last4=Li |first4=Zhengqun |last5=Rodriguez-Franco |first5=Marta |last6=Kraus |first6=Florian |last7=Bange |first7=Gert |last8=Albers |first8=Sonja-Verena |date=2018-02-06 |title=Structure and function of the archaeal response regulator CheY |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=115 |issue=6 |pages=E1259–E1268 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1716661115 |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=5819425 |pmid=29358409|bibcode=2018PNAS..115E1259Q |doi-access=free }}</ref> She has studied fossils of archaea, which provide evidence of at least 3.5 billion years of life on Earth.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Une vie motile dès 3.4 milliards d'années ? |url=https://www.insu.cnrs.fr/fr/cnrsinfo/une-vie-motile-des-34-milliards-dannees |access-date=2023-02-17 |website=www.insu.cnrs.fr |date=6 April 2021 |language=fr}}</ref>

Albers used [[cryogenic electron microscopy]] to unravel the structure of archaea thread.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Gaines |first1=Matthew C. |last2=Isupov |first2=Michail N. |last3=Sivabalasarma |first3=Shamphavi |last4=Haque |first4=Risat Ul |last5=McLaren |first5=Mathew |last6=Mollat |first6=Clara L. |last7=Tripp |first7=Patrick |last8=Neuhaus |first8=Alexander |last9=Gold |first9=Vicki A. M. |last10=Albers |first10=Sonja-Verena |last11=Daum |first11=Bertram |date=2022-12-01 |title=Electron cryo-microscopy reveals the structure of the archaeal thread filament |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=7411 |doi=10.1038/s41467-022-34652-4  |doi-access=free|pmid=36456543 |pmc=9715654 |bibcode=2022NatCo..13.7411G |issn=2041-1723}}</ref> Her work showed that the subunits of threads are interconnected via donor strand complementation, they have evolved differently from one another.<ref name=":2" />
